core: Working definition of ORDER BY, attributed: W3Schools says the ORDER BY keyword is used to sort the result-set in ascending or descending order

The basic shape: ORDER BY column at the end of a SELECT statement (W3Schools syntax SELECT column1, column2, ... FROM table_name ORDER BY column1, column2, ... ASC|DESC; and PostgreSQL tutorial example SELECT * FROM weather ORDER BY city;), with an original example SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price;

Ascending and descending: ASC is the default (W3Schools: sorts the result-set in ascending order (ASC) by default; PostgreSQL: ASC order is the default, smaller values first), DESC reverses the direction, with original examples

Sorting by more than one column: the first key is primary and later keys break ties (W3Schools Country-then-CustomerName example; SQLite: rows first sorted by the left-most ORDER BY expression, then ties broken by the second, and so on; PostgreSQL: later expressions sort rows equal on earlier values), with an original last_name, first_name example

Text sorts alphabetically, numbers sort by value (W3Schools alphabetical ProductName example vs lowest-to-highest Price example; PostgreSQL: ascending puts smaller values first per the comparison operator)

WHERE + ORDER BY together: WHERE clause processing filters the input data, then the ORDER BY clause sorts the remaining rows (SQLite four-step process; clause order WHERE before ORDER BY), with an original combined example; WHERE mechanics owned by the where sibling topic

Honest framing: ORDER BY affects the display order of the result set, not the stored data (PostgreSQL: sorting is a step applied after the query has produced its output table; without an explicit sort the row order is unspecified and must not be relied on)
supporting: Each sort key can have its own direction (W3Schools 'Combine ASC and DESC' example; PostgreSQL: each expression can be followed by an optional ASC or DESC keyword)
ORDER BY is one clause in SQLite's documented four-step SELECT result-generation process (FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY/HAVING/result-columns, DISTINCT)
outOfScope: LIMIT (own topic: limit — often paired with ORDER BY)
Indexes and performance tuning (own topic: indexes)
NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST and collation details (beyond literacy level)

claims.claim: W3Schools defines the ORDER BY keyword as the way to sort the result-set in ascending or descending order — the working definition for this lesson.
Ascending order is the default: W3Schools states the ORDER BY keyword sorts the result-set in ascending order (ASC) by default; writing DESC after a column requests descending order.

ORDER BY is written at the end of a SELECT statement, listing the column or columns to sort by; W3Schools gives the syntax SELECT column1, column2, ... FROM table_name ORDER BY column1, column2, ... ASC|DESC; and PostgreSQL's tutorial shows SELECT * FROM weather ORDER BY city;.

Multiple sort columns act as tie-breakers: W3Schools' example sorts by Country and then CustomerName (sorts first by Country, and if some records share a Country, sorts them by CustomerName); SQLite says rows are first sorted by the left-most ORDER BY expression, then ties are broken by the second expression, and so on; PostgreSQL says later expressions sort rows that are equal on the earlier values.

ASC and DESC can be set per sort column, and ASC is the default: PostgreSQL states each expression can be followed by an optional ASC or DESC keyword and that ASC order is the default, with ascending order putting smaller values first.

Text sorts alphabetically and numbers sort by value: W3Schools' examples order product names in descending alphabetical order and sort products from lowest to highest price; PostgreSQL defines ascending as smaller values first, where smaller is defined by the comparison operator.

Filtering happens before sorting: SQLite's SELECT reference describes generating results as a process in which WHERE clause processing filters the input data, and the ORDER BY clause then sorts the result rows; in the statement, ORDER BY comes after WHERE.

ORDER BY affects the display order of the result set, not the stored data: PostgreSQL describes sorting as a step applied after the query has produced its output table, guaranteeing the output ordering without changing the stored rows.

Without ORDER BY the row order of a query's result is unspecified: PostgreSQL warns that the actual order must not be relied on, and that a particular output ordering can only be guaranteed if the sort step is explicitly chosen.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources describe sorting at different levels: W3Schools speaks of sorting 'the result-set', PostgreSQL of an explicit sort step on the query's output table, and SQLite folds sorting into its four-step result-generation process.
positions: W3Schools: 'sort the result-set in ascending or descending order'
PostgreSQL: sorting is an optional step applied after the output table has been produced
SQLite: the ORDER BY clause sorts result rows within a documented processing order
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All three describe the same operation: ORDER BY arranges the rows a query returns, after filtering, without touching the stored table. The lesson uses W3Schools' result-set wording for the working definition (attributed) and PostgreSQL's output-table framing for the honest note that only an explicit sort guarantees an order.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Reused id from the phase-2 source registry with an identical URL. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: 'The ORDER BY keyword is used to sort the result-set in ascending or descending order'; 'sorts the result-set in ascending order (ASC) by default'; the syntax SELECT column1, column2, ... FROM table_name ORDER BY column1, column2, ... ASC|DESC;; the multi-column example SELECT * FROM Customers ORDER BY Country, CustomerName ('sorts it first by Country, and if some records have the same Country, it sorts them by CustomerName'); the DESC example SELECT * FROM Products ORDER BY ProductName DESC (descending alphabetical); the numeric example SELECT * FROM Products ORDER BY Price (lowest to highest); the 'Combine ASC and DESC' example. Used for the working definition, the default direction, multi-column sorting, and text-vs-number claims; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: PostgreSQL Documentation: 7.5. Sorting Rows (ORDER BY)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A official documentation. New id minted for this topic (not in the phase-2 registry). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: 'If sorting is not chosen, the rows will be returned in an unspecified order ... it must not be relied on. A particular output ordering can only be guaranteed if the sort step is explicitly chosen'; sorting happens 'after a query has produced an output table (after the select list has been processed)'; 'When more than one expression is specified, the later values are used to sort rows that are equal according to the earlier values'; 'Each expression can be followed by an optional ASC or DESC keyword ... ASC order is the default. Ascending order puts smaller values first, where "smaller" is defined in terms of the < operator'; the example SELECT a, b FROM table1 ORDER BY a + b, c;. Used for the unspecified-order warning, the display-not-stored framing, secondary keys, and ASC default claims.
